picks.why: St. Stefan ob Stainz family estate of the Weststeiermark, known by the farm's name vulgo Lex, which dates its first vineyards at Langegg to 1746 by its own account; its Schilcher Ried Hochgrail, the sharp rosé of Blauer Wildbacher from a high slope of gneiss, is the Weststeiermark's own wine at the single vineyard tier of the DAC, beside Schilcher from other Rieden and a sparkling one.
picks.note: Answered: the house bottles Schilcher from several Rieden, so the pick's wine was renamed to the Hochgrail (the swap above), house and key kept; the name Schilcher is protected for Styria's Blauer Wildbacher rosé since 1976. Open: the Hochgrail Reserve is left out, and 1746 is the family's account against a first written record of 1793. No living member of the family was met in the sources read.

swaps.why: no plain Egri Bikavér of the house was found in the listings read, while Pajados, a single vineyard Grand Superior by Ostoros, stands on the house, merchants and the Hungarian Wine Summit; house and key kept

picks.why: Egerszalók estate founded in 2002 in the Bükk foothills and named for the founder's wife, whose range is built around Bikavér; Merengő, its Superior, is a Kékfrankos led blend from several sites aged fifteen to seventeen months in 500 litre Hungarian oak, the tier beneath its single vineyard Grand Superior wines.
picks.note: Answered: 2002 stands on the house and Wines of Hungary; the blend in words is the house's for one vintage; Hangács and Nagy-Eged are in others. Open: the mix moves by vintage (Kadarka in 2022). The founder and his wife are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Noszvaj family house begun in 1984 on vineyards leased from the local council by Vilmos Thummerer (1943 to 2021), Hungary's Winemaker of the Year in 1995; its Grand Superior comes from a block on the limestone Nagy-Eged planted in 2008 with five varieties in the proportions of the blend, picked and fermented together as a field blend.
picks.note: Answered: the first vineyards were leased, not bought, in 1984; the label reads Egri Bikavér Grand Superior Nagy-Eged dűlő, and the Vili Papa cuvée is not taught. Open: the planting in the blend's proportions is the house's account. The founder is named with his dates; his widow and son are never named.

picks.why: Eger winery founded at the end of 1992 or in 1993 by Tibor Gál (1958 to 2005), who rose to chief winemaker at Tenuta dell'Ornellaia in Bolgheri after 1989 and died in a road accident in 2005; Pajados, a single vineyard Grand Superior by Ostoros on rhyolite tuff, is the leaner, firmer of the house's two site Bikavér, beside Síkhegy.
picks.note: Answered: Ornellaia, the founder's dates and his death on 10 February 2005 stand on Decanter; the plain Egri Bikavér could not be sourced, so the pick's wine was renamed to Pajados (the swap above), house and key kept. Founded stays empty between the end of 1992 and 1993. The son shares his father's name and the house's, so he is not listed in people.json; the record calls him the son.

picks.why: Eger house begun in 1998 by a first generation winemaker who planted the Öreghegy at Verpelét, its winery and cellars made in a disused stone quarry on the edge of the town; its Egri Bikavér is the first tier of the blend, Kékfrankos led and aged over a year in Hungarian oak, beneath its Superior and its Öreghegy Grand Superior.
picks.note: Answered: 1998 is the planting of the Öreghegy, with wine made at the quarry from 2003 by one profile. Open: the Hungarian Wine Summit calls the Öreghegy Grand Superior the house's flagship; the plan keeps the classic tier, and no rename was proposed. The founder is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Eger house founded in 1999 in the Nagykőporos cellar row, Count Buttler by its Hungarian name, which planted first on the volcanic Szarkás in 2000 and on the limestone Nagy-Eged from 2003, and passed to new owners in 2009; its Bikavér Superior from that hill shows the limestone side of the blend.
picks.note: Answered: the label reads Nagy Eged Bikavér Superior for 2018; the rules adopted in 1997 and official from 2002 are Magyar Bor's; the Kadarka Superior is in others. The count the house is named for is not told. Open: the 2018 sheet lists no Kékfrankos, and the bankruptcy said of 2009 is disputed and not told. The founding family, the former owner and the buyer of 2009 are never named.

swaps.why: the house's own page calls the Peres Cuvée, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc aged in new barrique from the Peres vineyard, its flagship, and the record teaches it under that name; the Irsai Olivér moves to others, ending its doubling with Bárdos és Fia; house and key kept

picks.why: Gyöngyös cellar in the Wine Palace, the Borpalota, whose story begins with a growers' co-operative of 1901 that became a share company in 1905; the family bought it in 2003 and gave it an old family surname, Dubicz, in 2016. Its Sárhegy Olaszrizling, from the volcanic Sár-hegy above the town and aged in Hungarian oak, is the fuller face of one of Hungary's most widely planted white grapes.
picks.note: Answered: founded stays empty (the co-operative of 1901, the family's purchase of 2003, the name of 2016); Olaszrizling is not the district's lead white grape, since Magyar Bor gives the Mátra's most grown as Irsai Olivér; the oak is set by vintage. Open: the fermentation vessel by vintage. The mother and daughter who run it are never named.

picks.why: Gyöngyöstarján family cellar built in 1947 by the great grandparents of the generation that runs it, by the house's account, and begun again after 1990; its Kékfrankos, from the tank fermented basic series, speaks for the Mátra as a new home of the grape, beside the old vine Hárslevelű its importers carry.
picks.note: Answered: the house counts four generations, not three; the rename to the Öregtokék Hárslevelű was refused by the refuter, since no source names it the flagship, its facts rest on single importers and it would double Losonci's grape. The family is never named.

picks.why: Small Gyöngyöspata family estate begun in 2004 by Magyar Bor's register, which adds no enzymes or cultured yeast; its Hárslevelű, from red andesite tuff north east of the village, shows the linden leaf grape of Tokaj on the Mátra's slopes.
picks.note: Answered thinly: no source names a flagship, and the record says so; the Hárslevelű is on Magyar Bor's register. A swap to the house's Rajnai Rizling, or to another Mátra house the review file names, was refused for now by the refuter and left to the integrator. The founder and that grower are listed in people.json; the house keeps its name and the prose says the family.

picks.why: Nagyréde family cellar begun in 1999, Bárdos and Son by its name, with its own vines on brown forest soil within the village; its Irsai Olivér, fermented cool in steel, is the light, scented spring white of the Mátra, the district that grows the grape more than any other.
picks.note: Answered thinly: no source names the flagship, and the Irsai Olivér stands as the wine the house is known by; 1999 is the house's account. The late owner is not named, his dates unknown, and the living family is never named.

picks.why: Gyöngyöstarján family cellar, making wine since the 1970s by its own account, whose founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year for 2017, the first from the Mátra; its Peres Cuvée, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc from the Peres vineyard at Gyöngyöspata aged in new barrique, first made in 2003 by the house's account, is the wine the house calls its flagship.
picks.note: Answered: the wine was renamed from the Irsai Olivér to the Peres Cuvée (the swap above), as the refuter ruled, since the house's own page calls it its flagship; the Irsai Olivér is in others. Open: the barrel months and the fermentation are not published, and the house gives no drinking window. The founder and his son are listed as the house only; the founder's status is unknown and he is never named in prose.

picks.why: Balf estate bought in 1997 by a Burgenland family of Blaufränkisch growers, who had first crossed into Hungary in 1992 with a winery at Villány; its Steiner, a single vineyard Kékfrankos from a slope of gneiss and mica schist called Spern Steiner at the purchase, is fermented with its own yeasts and aged two years in 500 litre barrels by the house's 2018 sheet.
picks.note: Answered: the soil is gneiss and mica schist by the house and Magyar Bor (stony schist), not the grey slate of one merchant; the estate was certified biodynamic in 2006, the Respekt group being founded only in 2007. Founded stays empty, since Balf was a purchase. Open: the 1680 chronicle and the Furmint for Ödenburger Ausbruch rest on the house; the son's start at Balf is 2000 in two accounts and 2002 in one. The family and its Villány partner are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Sopron family estate begun again in 1993, when the sisters' father bought land back with restitution vouchers after the grandparents had left for Austria, and run by two sisters since 2006; Újra Együtt, Together Again, is its Kékfrankos named for that return, aged eighteen months in small French oak by the house's 2022 note.
picks.note: Answered: the name's meaning is the family's account, and the making is the house's 2022 note rather than the lighter wine one account describes; the house's A világom közepe found no source and is not told. Open: the soils (limestone and slate, or volcanic) were not settled and stay out. The two sisters are listed in people.json; their father and his brothers are never named.

picks.why: Sopron house of red, white and sparkling wine, built since 1995 by its own account and dated 1997 by Magyar Bor's directory; its Chardonnay Brut is a traditional method blanc de blancs from the cool Kogl vineyard, given its second fermentation by the Szigeti house at Gols across the border.
picks.note: Answered: both years are told in the story and founded stays empty; the time on the lees is not published, so none is given. Open: one account calls the Brut a blend of the three Champagne grapes made only in exceptional years, while the house calls it a Chardonnay blanc de blancs, which the record keeps; the Gols arrangement rests on the house. The family is never named; the Szigeti brothers are listed in people.json.

picks.why: Small family winery in the hills between Fertőrákos and Balf, dated 2002 by Magyar Bor's directory and carried on by the founder's daughter after his sudden death; its Pinot Noir, wild fermented and rested in used barrels, shows the light, red fruited side of the lakeside climate beside the district's Kékfrankos.
picks.note: Answered: the refuter refused a rename to the house's Steiner Kékfrankos (no source says the house leads with it, and it would double Weninger's Steiner); the house grows Pinot Noir, Kékfrankos, Zweigelt and Cabernet Sauvignon, not Furmint. Founded stays empty, since 2002 rests on one directory. The daughter is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Fertőrákos house of a chef and winemaker, its restaurant opened in 1994 by the house's date in the family farmhouse on the village's main street, and the family winery taken over by the son in 2003; its Kékfrankos comes from a bare, chalky vineyard of the village, as Magyar Bor names it.
picks.note: Answered: no sweet wine of the house was found in any source, against the region record's line, which is reported and not edited; the restaurant's year is hedged (1992 in one account). Open: whether the house's Gneisz is the Kékfrankos Magyar Bor names was not settled, and the making is not published. The chef is listed in people.json and never named; his father's dates were not found.

swaps.why: the house bottles its Olaszrizling as Csobáncz Olaszrizling under the Balatoni name, by WineAlign, Wine Enthusiast and the house's press page, and the record teaches it under that name; the same house and the same wine, house and key kept

picks.why: Badacsonytomaj estate pieced together in the 1990s by Huba Szeremley (1940 to 2021), who came home after the change of regime and, with other growers, saved Kéknyelű from the last old plot at Nemesgulács; its Kéknyelű is the hill's rare native white, lean, smoky and slow to open.
picks.note: Answered: the revival was his with others, by Magyar Bor, not his alone; the auction of 2016 took his house and two vineyards, and the estate kept his name. Open: a cellar at Badacsonytomaj in 1992 rests on one obituary, so founded stays empty; the house's own cellar notes were not read, so the making gives the grape's. The son who runs the estate is never named.

picks.why: Badacsony family estate told from a wedding of 1978 at the Hableány hotel and the press house given to the couple, registered in 1990 by Magyar Bor, with its first labelled bottles in 1997 by its own account; its Szürkebarát is Pinot Gris in Badacsony's fuller way, one of the district's three traditional leading grapes.
picks.note: Answered thinly: no source names the house's flagship, so the Szürkebarát stands under the thin region rule, with the PiNO among the others. Open: whether this bottling carries Badacsony or Balatoni on its label. The founders and their children are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Badacsony estate founded in 2004 by two Swedish founders of the Sandahl family, which grows Rajnai Rizling alone on south facing slopes of the hill and ferments its parcels apart in steel; Rajnai Rizling, the true Riesling, makes its case on basalt, with Rare Peak as the house's premium grade.
picks.note: Answered: the house names no single flagship, so its Riesling is taught as the house's wine, with Oh Deer and the named cuvées in the label and the others; Falstaff lists the wines as Badacsony. Open: the Esterházy and Ranolder land is the house's claim, hedged; the first plantings of other grapes before Riesling are not told. The founders are never named.

picks.why: Estate at the foot of Csobánc founded in 2004 by a Swiss wine lover in the villa local accounts tie to the actress Klári Tolnay (1914 to 1998); its Csobáncz Olaszrizling, labelled Balatoni with the hill's old spelling and wild fermented with a long rest on its lees, shows the structure of a volcanic witness hill against the sandstone Olaszrizling of Csopak.
picks.note: Answered: the bottle is Balatoni Olaszrizling Csobáncz, so the pick's wine was renamed (the swap above), house and key kept, and no swap with Villa Sandahl's Riesling is needed; the Riesling of the Kápolna-domb is in others. Open: an older vintage was listed as Badacsony, so the label may have moved. The founder and the winemaker are never named.

picks.why: Csopak family house on the old estate of János Ranolder (1806 to 1875), Bishop of Veszprém, taken on in 1998 and among the Csopak producers who created the Csopak Codex in 2012; its Lőczedombi Olaszrizling comes from red Permian sandstone on Lőcze hill, and the house stands in the Balatonfüred-Csopak district, not in Badacsony.
picks.note: Answered: the Codex is Olaszrizling with at most a little Furmint, chosen by blind tasting; Ranolder White dates from 2002; the making is Magyar Bor's for 2024. Ruled on 2026-11-21: Jásdi stands, no swap. The refuter agreed in principle to a house of the Badacsony district itself (the Borbély cellar of Badacsonytomaj as a lead), but the Codex's own region record, Badacsony (Balaton), teaches the whole Balaton region: its summary names the six districts and Csopak's Olaszrizling to the east, and a card and a question teach Csopak and its charter, so a Csopak house teaches what the region covers, and the record says plainly that it stands outside the Badacsony district. Open: whether the label reads Csopak or Balatonfüred-Csopak. The founder and the Borbély family are listed in people.json and never named.

swaps.why: Grófi is the house's Hárslevelű site in every listing found, while Aranyhegy gives its oak aged single vineyard Juhfark, by bor.hu and the Parliament's wine page, and the record teaches it under that name; the same house and the same grape, house and key kept

picks.why: Somló estate begun in 2002 to make traditional method sparkling wine on the volcanic hill, with a sparkling wine cellar completed in 2011 and releases from 2014; Prestige Brut is Furmint and Chardonnay, its balance moved towards Chardonnay on the estate's recent sheet, and rests at least two years on its lees.
picks.note: Answered: the why is softened from a wine built on Furmint, as the refuter ruled; the time on the lees is told by sheet; the still Juhfark is in others. Open: the grape balance moves between releases. The founder and the cellar master from Champagne are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Somló family house that traces its start to 1946 and gathered vineyards across the southern slopes after 1990; its Aranyhegy Juhfark, a Selection wine fermented and aged in oak from the golden hill, is the hill's own grape from one named site, while the Grófi vineyard gives its Hárslevelű.
picks.note: Answered: Grófi is the house's Hárslevelű site in every listing, so the pick's wine was renamed to the Aranyhegy (the swap above), house and key kept; the label reads Somlói. Not told: the founder's co-operative and the first private bottling of 1982, found in one source only; the founder is described, his dates not found in two sources. Open: the Maria Theresa favour is told as a claim. The founder's son is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Small Somló family cellar on the south-eastern slope, bought by a postmaster great grandfather in the late nineteenth century, with its own wines from 2000 and its main building of 2008; its Juhfark, briefly on its skins, wild fermented and aged about a year or longer in large oak and acacia casks, is the hill's grape in the old, slow manner.
picks.note: Answered: the cask ageing is about a year for the 2019, one to three years in the cellar by the house, not the long cask ageing first supposed; the Parliament's wine of 2017 is told. Founded stays empty, since neither the cellar's purchase nor the first wines is a founding. The winemaker is never named; his name is also the house's legal name, carried in the Parliament's address; at the gates of batch B that address was ruled the house's own name (the lint keeps a listed name in an address where it carries the house's name and stands against a house word), and he is listed in people.json.

picks.why: Somló cellar begun in the early 1980s by its own account, in the early 1970s by others, by a winegrower known as the hill's grand old man, who made white wine alone and handed the cellar to a group of partners in 2014; its Somlói Juhfark, wild fermented in used thousand litre casks and released after three or four years, is the wine to know.
picks.note: Answered: the cellar began before 1990, so the why no longer calls it a house of the revival after communism, as the refuter ruled; Juhfark and Hárslevelű are both called its leading whites, Juhfark kept and Hárslevelű first in others. Founded stays empty. Open: one source puts the handover after the 2015 vintage, and a retailer says recent labels read Nagy-Somló. The founder and the three partners are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: The abbey cellar of Somló, on land the Benedictine Archabbey of Pannonhalma held vines on from 1811 and bought in 1901 by the cellar's account, broken up in 1948 and gathered again from more than twenty parcels by a group of partners from 2001, organic from 2017; its Nagy-Somlói Juhfark, wild fermented in Hungarian oak, is the hill's own grape.
picks.note: Answered: the tie to Pannonhalma stands on the cellar's own history; the 1911 sale and the Viennese vineyard are cut. Open: no sheet gives the Juhfark's time in cask. The vintner's grandson is listed in people.json and never named; neither is the founding partner of 2001.

picks.why: Villány family house whose Kopar, first made with the 1997 vintage after a Bordeaux journey and led by Cabernet Franc and Merlot since 2006, set the district's Bordeaux blend; it is named for the bare limestone Kopár slope of Szársomlyó.

picks.why: Kiskőrös family estate of three generations on the sand; Néró, a red grape bred at Eger that the family makes as a rosé, a barrel aged rosé and a siller, is the wine the house is known by.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run: the house is listed as Szentpéteri Borpince at Kiskőrös by the national wine marketing body (bor.hu and winesofhungary.hu); two accounts in English, a British drinks club's article and a Budapest business weekly, between them make Néró one of its leading grapes, made as a rosé, a red and a siller, and date the family's Néró programme to the early 2000s (the search summary did not say which account gives the date); an American wine guide's Hungarian pages list a Néró Rosé limited edition aged in wooden barrels (the 2018, in numbered bottles); and the Hungarian Parliament's wine pages name its Duna-Tisza közi Néró Rosé of 2021, from the Csábori Kétsor vineyard on a chalky base, a category winner. So the Néró found is bottled under Duna-Tisza közi, the plain's protected geographical indication and one of the names the region record covers, not under Kunsági: the author reads the label and says plainly which name it carries. The author chooses the Néró bottling the house leads with (the barrel aged rosé by the lane's account) and confirms the grape's parentage before writing it; the parentage was not searched in this run. bor.hu gives 2013 as the year of establishment beside a family history of three generations: leave founded empty unless two sources agree on what 2013 was. The region record's old vine Kadarka and Kékfrankos were not borne out; a Hungarian wine site has the house's Kadarka Blanc de Noir taking the sparkling wine prize of the Hungarian National Wine Contest of 2026, and it belongs among the others. The house writes itself Szentpéteri Borpince: confirm the label. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Soltvadkert family house with a wide range of the plain's whites, Irsai Olivér and the old Kövidinka among them, and fresh rosés; its Kunsági Kékfrankos Rosé is the dry rosé of the sand, sold widely at home.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. IN DOUBT on the wine, as the lane said. Confirmed in the thin run: Font Pincészet is a family winery at Soltvadkert by a tourism listing and by a Hungarian grocer's pages, which sell a Font Kékfrankos Rosé and a Font Irsai Olivér today and give its grapes as Irsai Olivér, Cserszegi Fűszeres, Kövidinka, Generosa, Ezerjó and Kékfrankos; a supermarket lists a Font Kunsági Kövidinka, so the house does bottle under the protected name. The rosé with a record abroad is a different one: by a search summary that drew on the national wine marketing body's article of July 2021 on the district's rosés, Font's Kunsági Cabernet Sauvignon Rosé 2020 took gold at Le Mondial du Rosé in Cannes, and the town's own paper of September 2018 reports a silver at Cannes for the family's Cabernet Sauvignon rosé of 2017; the author reads both before using either. The Kékfrankos Rosé is kept because it is the bottling shown on sale today and the lane found it under the Kunsági name, which this run did not see on a label, nor that it is dry; if the author finds that the Cabernet Sauvignon Rosé is the wine the house leads with and still makes, tell the read together agent, who changes the pick's wine. The refuter of chunk w28 refused that swap (the gold of 2020 not found on Wines of Hungary's own domain), and the Kékfrankos Rosé stands. No founding year and no history of the house was found in three searches: leave founded empty unless two sources give it, and write the story only from what is sourced. A politician of the same surname turns up in the same searches: name nobody living.

picks.why: Family estate of Szigetcsép on the Danube's Csepel island, far from the district's sandy core, its winery built in 2004 and one of the True Kunság cellars; its Kékfrankos Rosé, the 2019 a category winner among the Wines of the Hungarian Parliament, is the wine to know, the blended Rosé of Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The wines are entered as the district's: an international competition's results of 2024 give the Gál Rosé 2023 as Kunság, of Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, a Swedish sommelier's notes give the Kékfrankos Rosé of 2012 and of 2014 as Kunság, and the national tourism site sets the cellar among the True Kunság family wineries and says Szigetcsép lies far from the region's core. The lane's 1994 was not borne out: a listing that reads as the house's own words says the founders built the winery after some twenty years of work for other producers, so say nothing of 1994 unless two sources give it. Two rosés turn up, the blend sold as Rosé and a Kékfrankos Rosé (the 2019 a category winner among the Parliament's wines): the author confirms which the house leads with, the label's words and the protected name on it, and gives the blend in words with no yearly shares. The author still reads the Kunság specification for Szigetcsép among its communes, which this run did not open. Not the Gál Tibor estate of Eger, nor the Gál wineries of Villány. Swapped at the read together of chunk w28 from the blended Rosé to the Kékfrankos Rosé, as the author wrote the record and the refuter accepted, house and key kept. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Family estate between Izsák and Ágasegyháza whose head was a sparkling wine master at the Izsák sparkling works by another and which keeps to the plain's old grapes, Arany Sárfehér, Kövidinka, Ezerjó and Kadarka; its Brut is the sparkling wine it sells at home, little seen abroad.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line: the fifth pick, added in the thin run. IN DOUBT on the wine, and the merge agent rules. Confirmed, by search summaries of the national wine marketing body's article of July 2021 on the district and of the national tourism site's page on the estate, which the author reads to see which says what: the Gedeon estate near Kecskemét, its head a former sparkling wine master of the Izsák sparkling works who grows Kövidinka, Ezerjó, Sárfehér and Kadarka and makes sparkling wines and light wines with small bubbles; the tourism site also names Gedeon beside Font and Lantos among the district's houses; a business daily of 2012 sets the estate between Ágasegyháza and Izsák, growing Arany Sárfehér, Kövidinka, Ezerjó and Kadarka; and a Hungarian grocer sells a Gedeon Brut pezsgő, a Gedeon Extra Dry pezsgő and a Gedeon Irsai Olivér of 2024 today, their maker given as Gedeon Birtok Kft. of Gedeon dűlő, Izsák. Not confirmed, and the author settles each before writing: the grapes of the Brut (a wine database gives a Gedeon Birtok Cuvée, a sparkling wine filed under Kunság, as Rajnai Rizling, Arany Sárfehér and Zöldveltelini, and no source gives the Brut's), its method, and whether its label carries a protected name at all, Kunsági, Izsáki Arany Sárfehér or Duna-Tisza közi; a pezsgő may carry none. If it carries none, tell the read together agent, who moves the pick's wine to a wine of the estate that does, or rules on the pick. Little seen abroad rests only on this run finding no listing outside Hungary. No bottle sold as Izsáki Arany Sárfehér was found from this or any house in four searches, though the specification stands on the national authority's site (boraszat.kormany.hu) for still and sparkling wine of that one grape. The dates disagree: the estate built up since 1999 by one account, the company entered in November 2012 by a company register's mirror, so leave founded empty unless two agree; the accounts also disagree on the estate's size and its distance from Kecskemét, which no record needs. Standbys, none with a wine confirmed: Royalsekt, the Izsák sparkling works itself (founded in the 1950s and a sparkling plant since the 1970s by its trade fair profile on the wine body's site, its Arany Sárfehér pezsgő named in a consumer test of 2018 and not found on sale since), Lantos at Soltvadkert (2009 by bor.hu), and Polyák and Kunvin, both of which turned up on winesofhungary.hu in a search of the district's houses and were not looked into. The winery is entered here under its own name because the appellation has five bottlers this run could confirm and this is the fifth: the house's own page heads it Winery of Goumenissa, Domaine Filyria, and Wines of Greece lists it apart from the Naoussa cellar. Kept at the read together of chunk w28: the record takes the estate wine Filiria, never the Naoussa wines, and no sixth house of the zone stands ready; the Naoussa pick's note, which sent the Goumenissa to others, was set right at the gates of batch B and now sends it here. picks.why: The Macedonian house that took up Rapsani when its vineyards were close to abandonment and worked with the local growers to save the old vines and plant more, by the Greek wine body's account the appellation's only producer until 2005, until it stopped production in 2023; its Rapsani Reserve, the three grapes fermented together and aged in oak, carried the name abroad for a generation.

Ruled at the merge of 16 November 2026: the house is closed (production stopped in September 2023 and its bankruptcy was entered in the commercial registry on 12 January 2026, by two Greek business reports found in the thin run), and it stands in this group as history, because its Reserve is the Rapsani a sommelier is asked about and meets in old bottles. Write the whole record in the past tense, confirm the closure and its dates from two sources, and say nothing of what becomes of the brand. Do not propose a swap for the closure. Confirm that Rapsani Reserve was the label's own wording (beside a Grande Reserve, which goes in others), the ageing each term asked from the PDO's own text, and the house's founding (1890 is commonly given) from two sources. Tell its work with the growers as history with its dates.

picks.why: Family winery at the foot of Olympus, at Rapsani since 1991 and farmed organically by several accounts; its Rapsani Old Vines is the appellation's three grapes from old vines, aged in oak.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house also bottles a plain Rapsani (the 2023 is on sale in Britain) and a Rapsani named Tourtoura Old Vines (the 2020 reviewed by the same critic's site): confirm from the house which is the wine to know, and send the others to others with the Meth'Imon wines, whose appellation the author confirms. The dates disagree and the author settles them: at Rapsani since 1991 by several listings, organic from 1997 by one, and bottling the appellation's wine since 2008 by another, so leave founded empty unless two agree on what 1991 was. The lane's site name (Prosilia) was not confirmed, and the altitude (550 to 700 metres by the listings) is the house's own. The Ministry of Rural Development's file of an application to amend the Rapsani specification, named for 30 July 2026 and seen only through search summaries, names this house's company: read it before writing the making or the grapes' shares. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Rapsani family estate whose first vineyard was planted about 1935 by its own account, with a small winery set up after the third generation took over in 2002; its Rapsani is the three grapes fermented together and aged a year in old oak.

Confirmed in the thin run: the wine is sold as Rapsani by a Greek merchant and a British one (the 2021), and a British critic's site reviewed the 2019, the 2020 and the 2021 as Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto; the Greek merchant gives the three grapes fermented together and twelve months in old oak. About 1935 and the takeover of 2002 come from two merchants' profiles that read as the house's own words: hedge them as the house's account, and leave founded empty unless an independent source agrees. Sources write the house as Konstantinos Liapis, Liapis, Liapis Winery and Domaine Liapis: confirm the name the label carries, and that the label says PDO Rapsani. A Greek Master of Wine's account of 2016 has the head of this house working the vines of Terra Olympus, the Thymiopoulos company at Rapsani: say it only as two sources agree. Name no living person.

picks.why: The Rapsani company of the Naoussa house Thymiopoulos, set up about 2015 and, by one account, given its own cellar in a restored warehouse near Rapsani's railway station; Terra Petra is its Rapsani, Xinomavro with Krassato and Stavroto, sold under the Thymiopoulos name.

Thymiopoulos Vineyards is Naoussa's pick in plan.json (p-thymiopoulos), and that pick's note sends the Rapsani wine to others under the rule of one flagship a producer; the library's record of that house lists Rapsani Terra Petra among its wines. The company is entered here under its own name because three accounts make it a house of this appellation in its own right: a Greek Master of Wine's report of 2016 (the company is called Terra Olympus, and the 2016 vintage was to be made in its own winery in a restored warehouse near Rapsani's railway station), an importer's catalogue (established in 2015, when vineyards within the appellation came up for sale) and the Ministry of Rural Development's file of an application to amend the Rapsani specification, named for 30 July 2026 and seen only through a search summary, which names Terra Olympus of Rapsani. Keep producerId empty here. The wine is confirmed: Terra Petra is PDO Rapsani in an Austrian magazine's review of the 2015 and Rapsani in a British magazine's of the 2017 and the 2018, both under the Thymiopoulos name, and merchants in Greece and France stock the 2019 and the 2020. The author confirms what the label carries (Thymiopoulos, Terra Olympus or both), the grapes' shares (seven parts Xinomavro to three of Stavroto and Krassato by one Greek merchant, which sits beside the equal thirds the Codex's region record teaches: read the specification) and how the vines stand between this company and the Liapis family. Name no living person.

picks.why: A small family house at Rapsani's railway station, growing vines on Olympus for four generations by its own account and sold mostly in Greece; its Rapsani is the appellation's three grapes in equal shares, aged in oak and in bottle, made beside a Special Edition.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. IN DOUBT, thin: no search of the thin run showed the house at work after about 2022, and no merchant's listing of a recent vintage was found. What was confirmed: a blog post of 2009 that reads as the house's own announcement (growing and making wine since 1880, a fourth generation, a Rapsani of Stavroto, Krassato and Xinomavro aged twelve months in French oak); a Tempi tourism site's page on the wine route (gotempi.gr), which lists it at Rapsani beside Dougos and Liapis; a Greek travel site's guide of about four years ago (two labels, a Rapsani PDO red and a Rapsani PDO special edition, both aged in oak, and the address at Rapsani's railway station); and a Greek Master of Wine's note on the Rapsani 2009 Limited Edition, tasted in January 2020. The author confirms from the house that it bottles today, the label's own words and spelling (Chrisohoou in two sources, Chrysochoou in others), 1880 from a second source or leaves founded empty, and the blend. It is not the Chrysohoou estate of Naoussa, a different house whose wines turn up in the same searches. Tsantali, closed since 2023, stands in this group as history by the ruling at the merge. The only other bottler found is Boutari, whose own site lists a Rapsani of 2022, and Boutari is Naoussa's pick. Katsaros, which one glossary lists here, is at Krania, which has its own PGI. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: A house begun in 1986 at Pyrgela outside Argos and settled since 2004 in a winery at Malandreni, one of the two Argolid communes of the Nemea zone; the Grande Cuvée, Agiorgitiko alone from high vineyards and first bottled in 1996 by the house's account, is its Nemea.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run on the house's own pages (skouras.gr, read through search): founded in 1986 at Pyrgela, a village outside Argos, with rented vineyards; then a small winery at Gymno; then the winery at Malandreni in 2004, both villages inside the appellation, which Wines of Greece bears out (seventeen communes, fifteen in Corinthia with Gymno and Malandreni in Argolida). The house's sheet gives the wine as PDO Nemea, Agiorgitiko alone, first bottled in 1996, from vineyards at 1,040 metres; an American importer's listing adds red clay and twelve months in French barriques, half of them new. The vine age differs by merchant and the village of the vineyard was not found: confirm both from the technical sheet of the year taught. The label's word order varies on the house's own pages (Grande Cuvée Nemea on one, Nemea Grande Cuvée on another), so the pick holds Grande Cuvée alone, where the lane held Grande Cuvée Nemea: give the label in full. Megas Oenos, the first wine the house made, a blend of Agiorgitiko and Cabernet Sauvignon outside the appellation, goes in others with Saint George, its other Nemea. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Family estate at Ancient Nemea, by its merchants' accounts at work with Agiorgitiko since 1876 and among the district's first to farm organically; Palaia Klimata, Old Vines on the export label, is Agiorgitiko alone from an old section of its vineyard, held long in oak and bottle.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run on the house's own label pages (papaioannouwines.gr, read through search): Palaia Klimata, Old Vines in English and Vieilles Vignes in French, Nemea PDO, Agiorgitiko alone, made at the family winery at Ancient Nemea from a chosen section of vines about forty years old, with eighteen months in oak and a year in bottle; a British merchant gives at least twelve months in French oak and twelve in bottle, so tell the regime by vintage. The house's German page spells it Palea Klimata. The year 1876 and the early organic farming come from merchants and Greek guides, not from a house page seen: hedge 1876 as a claim or leave founded empty, and confirm the certification before saying certified. The lane's line that the estate was among the first of the district to bottle its own wine was not tested in the thin run: say it only with two sources. Microclima, as the house spells its Nemea from a single plot, goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: The Nemea estate of the Mantinia house Tselepos: a vineyard of old Agiorgitiko at Koutsi bought in 2003 and named Ktima Driopi, with a small winery of its own; the Reserve, Agiorgitiko alone with a year in French oak, is its Nemea for the cellar.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run on the family's own pages (tselepos.gr, read through search): 2003 is the purchase of the estate at Koutsi and the founding of Ktima Driopi; the vines were about fifty years old by the house (thirty five by one merchant), a part was replanted with clean Agiorgitiko and a small winery was built on the estate. The house lists the wine as Ktima Driopi Reserve, Nemea PDO, Agiorgitiko alone, twelve months in French oak, seven tenths of it new, and six months in bottle, from a vineyard it places at Dourmiza in Koutsi. The spelling is Driopi on the house's pages and Dryopi at a Greek merchant. The house gives the estate 380 metres and an American merchant about 1,250 feet: use the house's figure. The same family as the Mantinia pick Tselepos: a separate estate with its own name and wine, which the record says plainly. Driopi Classic, Cava Driopi and the rosé go in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Small family winery at Petri, begun in 1997 by two accounts and in 1996 by a third, its chosen vineyards kept to low yields and given little fertiliser; Monopati, the first of its premium wines by a Greek merchant's account, is Agiorgitiko alone under the appellation, aged in French oak.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. Confirmed in the thin run: Monopati is sold as PDO Nemea, Agiorgitiko alone, by a Greek merchant and written up as Nemea by a Greek Master of Wine and on a British critic's site (the 2021: vines at 550 metres, twenty five days on the skins). The lane's 1996 is one merchant's year; a Greek food guide and the Greek Master of Wine give 1997: leave founded empty unless the house settles it. The vineyard: one plot at Daouliza in Koutsi since the 2014 vintage and Sikitsa before it, by the Master of Wine's notes; vines more than fifty years old by one merchant and nearing fifty by another: confirm both. The oak is fourteen or sixteen months in French barrels by vintage, and the wine is unfiltered by one listing. Whether the vineyard is certified organic is contested between listings: say dry farmed and no more. The wine named 4, from a vineyard said to predate phylloxera, Le Sang de la Pierre, Armakas and the estate Nemea go in others; confirm that Monopati and not 4 is the wine a guest meets. A father founded the house and his son, trained in Burgundy, makes the wine: name neither.

picks.why: Family winery founded in 1995 at Ancient Nemea, a short walk from the sanctuary, with a range that runs from a plain Nemea to regional blends; Ammos Terra Leone is its oak aged Nemea, Agiorgitiko alone from the family's own vineyard at Kokkinies.

Added in the thin run as the fifth pick, because Gaia Wines is Santorini's pick and Semeli is Mantinia's. Confirmed on the house's own pages (palivos.gr, read through search): a family winery founded in 1995 at Ancient Nemea, when a modern winery took the place of the old treading tank, 800 metres from the archaeological site; Ammos Terra Leone is a dry red PDO Nemea of Agiorgitiko alone from the family's vineyard at Kokkinies and Stefani. A British merchant and a Greek wine magazine also date the house to 1995; one account says the vineyards had been the family's for a century and a half: hedge it. The label's words vary: Ammos Terra Leone on the house's pages and at a British merchant for the 2022, Terra Leone Ammos Reserve on a British critic's site for the 2020, Terra Leone Single Vineyard Selection Ammos Reserve in an Austrian magazine for the 2006, so the pick holds Terra Leone alone: give the label in full for the years taught, and say Reserve only where the label does. The ageing differs between the house's two pages (eighteen months in French oak and six in bottle; fourteen months in new French oak and amphorae and eight in bottle) and a merchant gives the 2014 eighteen months in new oak, four fifths French and a fifth American: tell it by vintage. Noema, the house's blend of Agiorgitiko, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, is PGI Peloponnese and never its Nemea; it goes in others with Palivou Estate Nemea, the plain wine of the appellation. The house writes Palivou in English and Palivos in its address. Organic and biodynamic farming is a merchant's word: confirm before saying so. A founder and his two daughters appear on the house's pages: name none of them. Should a pick fall, the standby is the Nemea Wine Cooperative, founded in 1937 by retailers' accounts, whose Nemea Grande Reserve a British grocer sells as PDO: not confirmed on a page of its own.

picks.why: Family estate outside Rizes near Tripoli, founded in 1989 by an oenologist who had settled on the plateau in 1981 and worked first as a consultant; its Mantinia, Moschofilero from the high plateau, is the reference a sommelier is expected to know for the appellation.

Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Small family winery at Thiramonas below Mount Ainos, selling its wine since 2002 by two merchants' accounts, first under the Melissinos name and later under the family's own, Petrakopoulos; Robola Natural Palia Armakia, from two old vineyards of ungrafted Robola at Fagia, fermented with its own yeasts and bottled unfiltered with very little sulphur, is the appellation's low intervention face.
