Swapped on 21 November 2026 from Melissinos Natural Robola to Petrakopoulos Robola Natural Palia Armakia, the swap the refuter of chunk w18 accepted: one house renamed, key kept. The family history, the 1950 Zakynthino, the 1953 earthquake, the vineyards and the making rest on the house's own pages and are hedged as its account; 2002 rests on two merchants; the year of the renaming was not found. The meaning of Armakia and bottle numbers stay out. Name no living founder.

picks.producer: Union of Winemaking Cooperatives of Samos
picks.why: The growers' co-operative union founded in 1934, the appellation's only producer until 2016 by Wines of Greece, with wineries at Malagari and Karlovasi; Samos Vin Doux, White Muscat fortified early with grape spirit, is the plainest and freshest of its sweet wines.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; the region record's producers line names the house, a lead and no proof. Confirmed in the thin run: 1934 on the co-operative's own history page (samoswine.gr, read through search) and at Wines of Greece, which adds that it began with twenty six local co-operatives and that it was the only producer of the appellation until 2016, private wineries working beside it since; the island's wine routes guide names its two wineries, at Malagari by the town of Samos and at Karlovasi. Samos Vin Doux is listed under that name by a British magazine and a Canadian critic. The house's name differs by source: Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos (EOSS) at Wines of Greece, United Winemaking Agricultural Cooperative of Samos or UWC Samos in the wine routes guide and on the listings; the pick keeps the name the region record uses: give the name the label prints, and say when the union took its later form only if two sources date it. Wines of Greece gives the appellation three types: vin naturellement doux from sun dried grapes, vin doux naturel, fortified, with Grand Cru for fruit grown above 400 metres, and vin doux; that the Vin Doux is a vin de liqueur, fortified at or near the start of fermentation, rests on the region record and one taster's note: confirm it on the appellation's specification. Grand Cru, Nectar, of sun dried grapes, and Anthemis, aged in oak, go in others. Shares, volumes and exports stay out.

picks.why: Family winery at Karlovasi, opened in 2013 by the island's wine routes guide and a merchant's account, of a family that came from Malta in the nineteenth century and traded the island's Muscat; Nopera Vintage is its sweet Samos of sun dried Muscat.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. Confirmed in the thin run: the island's wine routes guide (samoswineroutes.gr, read through search) places the winery at Karlovasi, dates its opening to 2013 and tells of a family that left Malta in the middle of the nineteenth century, made wine of White Muscat on Samos and later traded it abroad; a merchant's page also gives 2013, as the year the house became the first modern private winery. No page of the house's own was reached: hedge the family's story as the house's account, and leave founded empty unless 2013 stands on the house's own page. That it was the first private winery of Samos since 1934 is the guide's and that merchant's line, and Vakakis is dated 2011: hedge it or leave it out. Nopera Vintage is sold under that name by a Greek merchant (the 2013) and by a British importer of Greek wine (the 2017: ripe Muscat dried in the sun, then fermented slowly), and listings place it under PDO Samos; a Greek Master of Wine's site lists it as Nopera with the year alone and gives the 2014 about two years in French oak, and a British magazine lists it as Nopera, Samos: give the label in full for the year taught and confirm the appellation on it. Epitome, the house's other sweet wine, and Roya, its dry Muscat, which the lane held to be a wine of geographical indication outside the sweet appellation, go in others; confirm what Epitome is, since one listing runs it together with the Vintage of 2013, and confirm Roya's category. The guide's three vineyards and their size stay out. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Private winery near Karlovasi that began in 2011, while the law of 1934 still bound the island's growers to the co-operatives; Epogdoon, its Samos of sun dried White Muscat, is named for the interval of nine to eight in the Pythagorean theory of music.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. Confirmed in the thin run: two accounts, a Greek merchant's and a tour guide's, date the house to 2011, when the law of 1934 still obliged the island's growers to deliver their grapes to the co-operatives, and say its founder fought that rule in the Greek and the European courts: tell the lawsuit only with a source that names the case, and say what the house bottled before 2016, which no search showed. The village differs by source: the island's wine routes guide places the winery at M. Lakka, on the road from Karlovasi to Konteika, and a travel guide files it under Vathy: follow the wine routes guide. Epogdoon is listed as PDO by a British merchant (the 2016, Muscat Blanc alone) and under Samos on a British critic's site (the 2017, there called Pythagorean Epogdoon Barrel): a barrel aged bottling stands beside the plain one, so say which is taught and give the label in full. The name, by the Greek merchant quoting the house: the epogdoon is the interval of nine to eight on which the Pythagorean theory of music rests, chosen for a partly sun dried wine of White Muscat; the same page says about eight kilos of fruit give one litre: confirm both on the house's own page. The lane's line that the house is known for reviving Black Muscat was not tested: say it only with two sources. Filion, listed under Samos on the same critic's site, and Kalypso go in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Small family winery at Marathokampos, at work since 2016 among the terraces of the family's estate; its Samos, sold under the appellation's name alone, is a naturally sweet wine of sun dried White Muscat aged at least three years in barrel, by the house's account.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. Added in the thin run as the fourth pick. Confirmed on the house's own pages (coutsodontiswinery.gr, read through search): small lots made since 2016 on a family estate at Marathokampos among traditional terraces; the wine is headed Samos Naturally Sweet Wine in English and Samos, oinos fysikos glykys, in Greek, the 2017 of Muscat Blanc from small terraces at 100 to 300 metres, the grapes laid in the sun before pressing, fermented in stainless steel and aged at least three years in barrels. The island's wine routes guide also dates the family winery to 2016 and places it at Marathokampos. No merchant, critic or competition listing of the wine was found, so the record would rest on the house's pages alone: hedge every figure as the house's account. The letters PDO were not seen: the page gives the appellation's name and the legal words for its sun dried type, which Wines of Greece lists under PDO Samos, so confirm the appellation on the label before the record says it. The pick holds Samos alone because the wine has no other name: give the label in full. Its dry White Muscat, its aged dry White Muscat, its orange wine and its pétillant naturel go in others: confirm each one's category, since none can be the sweet appellation's wine. The house writes Coutsodontis; a Greek news guide writes Koutsodontis. No listing off the island was found: the record says plainly that this is a small young house, little seen abroad on what was read. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Young family estate at Mytilinii in the centre of the island, founded in 2019, farming organically and making only White Muscat, dry and naturally sweet; Anavasis is the wine it bottles as Samos, young and from a wild ferment by a merchant's listing.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line. Added in the thin run as the fifth pick, and the one in doubt. Confirmed: the island's wine routes guide (samoswineroutes.gr, read through search) dates the winery to 2019 at Rizovrachos, Mytilinii, in central Samos, a father and his two sons working organic vineyards and making only dry and naturally sweet wines of White Muscat in numbered bottles; the estate's own page (hatziioannouestate.gr, read through search) calls it a family house given wholly to organic wines. Anavasis: the results of the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles list Hatziioannou, Samos, Anavasis 2021 as a still wine of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, appellation Samos, organic and not oaked; a wine app names it Samos with the wine's name in Greek; a delicatessen that sells the island's wines online lists Anabasis in a half litre bottle as an organic Samos, young and fermented by native yeasts alone. No page read says PDO or sweet of this wine outright: the case rests on the name Samos on the label, which only the appellation's wine may carry, on the competition's appellation field, on the half litre bottle and on the estate's naturally sweet wines. Confirm on the estate's own page or the label that Anavasis is PDO Samos and which of the appellation's types it is; if it is not, the pick falls. Antamoma, also written Rendezvous, its dry White Muscat, goes in others. The spelling is Anavasis at the competition and Anabasis at the delicatessen; the house is Hatziioannou on its own pages and Hatzigiannou in a Greek news guide, and a retailer's dry Muscat of Chatziioannou Domaine may be the same estate or another house: keep them apart until shown. The medal stays out. Name no living member of the family. Should the pick fall, no sixth house of the appellation was found: of the seven the wine routes guide lists, Kostaki, whose first vintage was 2023, makes dry and sparkling Muscat by a Greek merchant and a British magazine, and nothing was found on the wines of Eleftheriou at Stavrinides; the Samos bottled by the mainland houses Kourtaki and Cavino, seen in Canadian listings, was not tested and is a label from off the island.

picks.why: The Keuka Lake house founded in 1962 as Vinifera Wine Cellars by a Ukrainian born plant scientist who showed that grafted vinifera could live through Finger Lakes winters; its Dry Riesling is the bottle that carried that argument.
picks.note: Answered: 1962 as Vinifera Wine Cellars by the house's homepage and sales packet, the land of 1958 by the house; the founder's dates 1899 to 1985 by two biographies (1897 in one Russian source, left open); the hiring at Gold Seal dated 1953 by the house. The Dry Riesling's fruit is the house's own blocks on Keuka Lake, planted from 1958, and on Seneca Lake, from 2007, by its sheets of 2018 to 2024. The Rkatsiteli and Chateau Frank are in others; no living member of the family is named.

picks.why: Seneca Lake estate founded at Dundee in 1979 by a Mosel born grower, whose nursery grafted vines for growers across the East; the HJW Vineyard Riesling, the single vineyard wine that carries the founder's initials, is the house's Riesling to know.
picks.note: Answered: 1979 by the house and Wikipedia, with Wine Spectator's 1981 for the first wines sold told beside it; the HJW Vineyard is the founder's shale site above the west shore of Seneca Lake near Dundee, planted from 1976 to 1978 by the house's sheet; the wine is dry or close to it, about 6 to 7 grams a litre by merchants. No death of the founder was found, so he is treated as living and said as the founder; the house keeps its name, so Hermann J. Wiemer is not listed in people.json. The Dry Riesling and the Magdalena Vineyard Riesling are in others.

picks.why: A house begun on the steep eastern slopes of Keuka Lake, its cellar later moved to Geneva, making dry Riesling and Cabernet Franc from Keuka and Seneca fruit; the Argetsinger Vineyard Dry Riesling, from a steep Seneca Lake site of the early 1980s on gravel over limestone, is the one to know.
picks.note: Answered: 2001 by the house's sheet and Decanter, 2000 for the land by two others; the Argetsinger Vineyard lies on the southeast shore of Seneca Lake below Burdett, on Howard gravel over limestone, planted in the early 1980s and owned and farmed by the Argetsinger family, by the house's pages and Skurnik. The why's Keuka Lake house is set right, since the record moves the winemaking to Geneva, and its one of the old vineyards of Seneca Lake is set right as a site of the early 1980s. No living person is named: the founding couple.

picks.why: A vineyard on the east shore of Seneca Lake given almost wholly to Riesling and bottled by clone and by sweetness; No. 239 Dry Riesling is a single clone wine of Geisenheim clone 239, a lesson in what a clone brings to a glass.
picks.note: Answered: the estate dates from the sale of 2008 and the vineyard from 2009 by the house's history page and FAQ, at Lodi near the east shore of Seneca Lake; first wines released in 2013 by the house. No cellar is named as maker. The clones bottled apart, 239 for the dry wine and 198 for the reserve, are the house's; the label form No. 239 is the merchants' and the plan's (the house writes Riesling Dry 239). No living person is named.

picks.why: A Seneca Lake house founded with a partner from the southern Rhône, making bone dry Riesling and Pinot Noir in a European idiom; the Classique Dry Riesling, blended from sites on the east shore of the lake, is its wine to know.
picks.note: Answered: 2011 by Decanter, the importer's sheet and a merchant's page; a partnership with a grower of the family of Château de Saint Cosme, no partner named; Forge Cellars a house of its own. The label reads Dry Riesling Classique on the house's pages, a rename for the integrator, not a swap; ten to sixteen east shore sites by vintage on the house's pages (thirteen in Decanter); since 2014 refuted by a 2013 Classique and cut. The Classique Pinot Noir and the single sites are in others.

picks.why: Cutchogue estate on the North Fork, planted from 1980 by the region record's account, whose Merlot and blends of the Bordeaux grapes set the serious end of the fork; Musée, its blend of those grapes, is the wine of the house.
picks.note: Answered: planted in 1980 by the house's Heritage page; the sale dated 1999 by the house and 2000 by Wine Spectator and Dan's Papers, both taught. Musée's grapes change yearly, Merlot led in most vintages, by the house's listings; Chuck Close's label for the first Musée, the 2005, by Dan's Papers; the daguerreotype of the picked grapes found in no source and cut. The Merlot and Taste Red are in others; no living person is named.

picks.why: Peconic estate planted in 1978, one of the early vineyards of the North Fork; its Old Vines Merlot, from the oldest vines and held back for years before release, is the house's red to know, the wine of a house that set its bottles beside Europe's in comparative blind tastings.
picks.note: Answered: 1978 at Peconic and the change of hands of 1988 by 27 East, Long Island Wine Country and the house, the buyers left unnamed as accounts differ; the library begun after 1993 and the Old Vines tier made only in strong vintages by the house. The why's blind tastings that first set Long Island beside Bordeaux are set right: no source dated them or tied them to Bordeaux, so the record says comparative blind tastings, undated. The Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon and the Estate Selection Merlot are in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Aquebogue on the North Fork since 1983 and one of the few on Long Island to grow Chenin Blanc; its Chenin Blanc is the North Fork white a sommelier is asked about.
picks.note: Answered: 1983 at Aquebogue by Grape Collective, RiverheadLOCAL and the Wine Folly guide; the Chenin Blanc found in an abandoned vineyard bought in 1989 and planted further in 2000 and 2005, by northforker and Grape Collective; dry, unoaked and fermented cool in steel. The first Chenin of New York is the house's claim and the screw caps of 2007 the local press's, each told so. The Riesling and the Cabernet Sauvignon are in others; the family is said, no member named.

picks.why: The South Fork's landmark at Sagaponack, planted from 1988 by its Hamburg born founder; its pale, dry Estate Rosé, a Merlot led blend of several grapes, grew with the Hamptons' taste for rosé.
picks.note: Answered: the land of 1978, the planting of 1988 as Sagpond Vineyards, the first Sagpond rosé of 1993 and the renaming and first Estate Rosé of 1996 by the house's timeline (1997 for the renaming by 27 East and VinePair); the founder's death on the last day of 2008 by Decanter and 27 East, so he is not named and is left undated. The why's made in the Provence manner is set right: no source read says so, and the record teaches a Merlot led blend, picked in waves and given time on its lees. Summer in a Bottle is a separate line; Christian's Cuvée Merlot is in others.

picks.why: A Mattituck estate on the Long Island Sound, planted in 1995 on a family farm and worked with biodynamic methods; Bergen Road, its blend of the Bordeaux grapes, is the house's red to know.
picks.note: Answered: Bergen Road is the house's flagship red, made only in strong vintages, by the house's pages; Alexandra, the reserve red, is in others. Planted in 1995 by father, son and daughter in law, and farmed biodynamically from the first plantings with the family's own compost and a herd for the preparations, by the house's family page and the Wine Folly guide. The origin of the name Bergen Road is not taught. No living member of the family is named.

picks.why: Orange County estate founded in 1976 by a Veneto wine family beside the ruins of a house Thomas Jefferson designed; Octagon, its blend of the Bordeaux grapes named for the house's eight sided room and made only in chosen years, is the Virginia red a sommelier is asked about.
picks.note: Answered: 1976 by the house's Heritage page and two others; Governor James Barbour's house, built to Jefferson's designs and complete by about 1822, burned on Christmas Day 1884, by Virginia's historic resources body and the Monticello encyclopedia. Octagon is named for the eight sided room, first made in 1991, again in 1995, and in quantity from 1998 by the press; Merlot led in most vintages read, Cabernet Sauvignon led in 2007; made only in chosen years. The Veneto family is said; its Italian grapes are in others.

picks.why: Orange County estate that led Virginia's turn to Viognier in the early 1990s and brought the native Norton back into commercial use; its Viognier is the white that first made the state's name.
picks.note: Answered: the land at Gordonsville bought in 1989 after a home vineyard of 1983, the first crop of 1991 made at Montdomaine and the first crush of 1993, by the house's About page and Wikipedia; the competition is the San Diego National of 1994, where the 1992 Viognier won its class by the house's medal list, not a 1993 win. The founding year is left empty. The founder's death in 2018 rests on the author's two sources, so he is said and not named. The Norton, the Petit Manseng and the Rkatsiteli are in others.

picks.why: A Blue Ridge estate in Fauquier County known for wines drawn from its own mountain slopes; the Hardscrabble Chardonnay, from the home vineyard of that name, is the house's white to know, beside a Hardscrabble red.
picks.note: Answered: the Hardscrabble Chardonnay is taught and the Hardscrabble Red goes in others. The orchard bought in 1983, the first vines of 1985 and the first commercial vintage of 1987, at about 1,350 feet on the Blue Ridge, by the house's About and Hardscrabble pages; the founding year is left empty as the record has it. No living person is named: the founder and his family.

picks.why: A Delaplane estate in the Blue Ridge foothills of northern Virginia making two Bordeaux style reds from its own slopes; Lost Mountain, the Cabernet Sauvignon led one, is the house's flagship.
picks.note: Answered: Lost Mountain is the house's Cabernet Sauvignon led grand wine (Cabernet Franc leads in some years) and Rendezvous, Merlot led, its other, by the press; first vintage 2008 in every account, the land of 2004 by most (2006 in one), so the founding year is left empty; thin gravelly topsoil over decomposed granite. The sale of June 2024 and the new name Lost Mountain Vineyards are history told with its year; the producer is still labelled RdV Vineyards here, a relabel for the integrator with the key kept, not a swap. No living person is named.

picks.why: A northern Virginia estate given to Norton, the native grape raised in Richmond in the 1820s, and to Albariño; its Norton is the state's own red grape in an estate's hands.
picks.note: Answered: the label is Locksley Reserve Norton, the house's reserve red, its 2021 gold at the Virginia Governor's Cup of 2024 by Middleburg Life, Northern Virginia Magazine and the house; Norton first planted at the Locksley Estate in 1998; the founding year left empty. The largest single planting of Norton anywhere is the house's claim, told so. The Albariño and the Estate Bottled Norton are in others; the Viognier is named in the story only. No living person is named: the founder.

picks.why: Molinos estate in the upper Calchaquí, founded in 1831 and one of Argentina's oldest working wineries; Altura Máxima, Malbec from a vineyard at roughly 3,100 metres, puts the altitude of the Calchaquí in one bottle.
picks.note: Answered: 1831 by the house's brochure, with the founder's governorship of 1809 and 1810 by two sources, his dates not found, so he is described. Altura Máxima is the house's Malbec of the Payogasta vineyard at about 3,111 metres by the house, first made in 2012; the vineyard's planting year differs (2004, or 2007 to 2009) and is not taught. The purchase of 2001 is told as history; no living person named. The Estate Malbec and the Torrontés are in others.

picks.why: Cafayate house founded in 1892, the valley's historic cellar, with old vines of Torrontés, Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon; the Old Vines 1945 Torrontés, named for the year its parcel was planted, shows the valley's grape from old vines.
picks.note: Answered: the Michel brothers began making wine in the valley in 1892, not on the La Rosa estate, which Mercado dates to 1925; the Michel Torino name told as history, the family's sale of the 1990s or about 2000 and the Peñaflor purchase and the name El Esteco of 2004 by three sources. 1945 is the parcel's planting year on Finca Las Mercedes by the house. The vessel is left out for want of a second source. The other Old Vines wines are in others.

picks.why: A long established Cafayate house, wine first made at La Florida in 1850 by the house's account and the winery bought in 1938 by the man who married into the founding family, whose surname it carries; a name for Torrontés in dry and late harvest styles, and Arnaldo B., the red of 1990 named in his honour, is the house's flagship.
picks.note: Answered: 1850 at La Florida, the purchase of 1938 and the launch of Arnaldo B. in 1990 by the house's English and Spanish pages and sheets, Bichos de Campo and MDZ; the buyer of 1938 described, not named, his dates found nowhere. The sale to Pernod Ricard told as the middle of the 1990s, the sources differing between 1995 and 1996; a later sale left out. San Pedro de Yacochuya is its own pick; the dry and late harvest Torrontés are in others.

picks.why: Small estate in the hills above Cafayate at about 2,000 metres, where the Etchart family worked with a Bordeaux consultant from 1987 or 1988 and built a winery in 1998; Yacochuya, its dense Malbec from old vines, first made in 1999, is one of Argentina's early Malbecs made for the cellar.
picks.note: Answered: the consultant brought to the valley in 1987 or 1988, the accounts differing, the winery built from 1998 and the first vintage of February 1999 by CellarTracker and Welcome Argentina; the release of 1990 by one account not taught. The height is about 2,000 metres by two sources (6,700 feet, more than 2,000 metres); the vines more than sixty years old by two accounts, older by others. The consultant is not named. The San Pedro de Yacochuya red and Coquena are in others.

picks.why: A restored historic family cellar in Cafayate making Torrontés and reds of Malbec and Tannat from the valley's sandy soils; Laborum names its single vineyard wines, its Torrontés the house's white to know.
picks.note: Answered: Laborum is the house's range of single vineyard wines of one variety, and the Finca El Retiro Torrontés the one taught, the refuter keeping the pick over the Porvenir blend at the head of the range. The cellar told as built by Italian immigrants early in the twentieth century by one guide; the family's purchase of 2000 by two guides. No living person named.

picks.why: The co-operative of grower families at Chilecito in the Famatina Valley, at work since 1940; Santa Florentina, the range named for an old mining village near the cellar, carries its Torrontés Riojano, the white grape named for the province.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run: 1940 and Chilecito from the co-operative's own pages (la-riojana.squarespace.com, read through search) and from Argentine press (mercado.com.ar, bichosdecampo.com); one academic paper says it began as an offshoot of the Córdoba co-operative La Caroyense: confirm before saying so. The range name Santa Florentina and its village, about twelve kilometres from the winery, come from the house's own page: confirm the Torrontés of the range is Famatina fruit and give the label in full. The lane held Torrontés alone; the house also sells Tilimuqui, its organic Fairtrade range from the Famatina, which goes in others. Member numbers differ by source (about 360, 400, 500): leave them out. Name no living person, the winemaker included.

picks.why: A young estate at about 1,700 metres in the Chañarmuyo valley at the north of the Famatina, begun in 2001, when its founder bought the land, and selling its own wine since about 2006; the Estate Malbec, labelled with its height, is its red of altitude.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run: the estate in the Famatina Valley and its high viticulture by the national tourism board (argentina.travel); planting from 2001 by a wine tourism directory; wine made and sold since 2006 at 1,720 metres by an academic case study (revistarivar.usach.cl); an American merchant lists the Estate Grown Malbec at 1,700 metres, and Delectable lists an Estate Malbec and a Reserva Malbec. No source seen confirms a Torrontés from the estate: do not say it makes one without the house. The national board names the Tannat of its Gran Vino Reserva line as its most awarded wine: an award is never told, but confirm with the house which wine it leads with, and give the label as the bottle has it. Height differs between 1,700 and 1,720 metres: give about 1,700. The founder is living: name only the family.

picks.why: A house with a cellar and vineyards in the Castro Barros valley, on the far side of the Sierra de Velasco from the Famatina, and a second winery at Vistalba in Luján de Cuyo; its La Rioja Torrontés shows the province's grape from another valley.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; not in the region record. Confirmed in the thin run: the La Rioja winery in the department of Castro Barros and the Mendoza winery at Vistalba by Wine Folly's guide and a wine tourism directory; an academic case study (revistarivar.usach.cl) places the firm at Anillaco and others at Aminga, both towns of Castro Barros: confirm which town the cellar stands in. Wine.com lists San Huberto La Rioja Torrontés, and the house sells an Aminga range named for the valley: confirm the Torrontés label taught is La Rioja fruit, not Mendoza, and give it in full. The founding year was not found: leave it empty unless the house gives it. Name no living person.

picks.why: A family estate of vines and olive groves at Vichigasta, south of Chilecito between the Famatina and Velasco ranges, begun in 1994 with a winery built in 2002 by its own account; La Puerta Torrontés is its white.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; not in the region record. Confirmed in the thin run: the house on the province's tourism list of bodegas (turismo.larioja.gob.ar), at Vichigasta in the Chilecito department, and by Time Out and Argentine press (bichosdecampo.com); 1994 and 2002 come from one wine tourism directory only: confirm both from the house or hedge them as its claim. Wine.com lists La Puerta Torrontés and La Puerta Alta Bonarda; a British critic's tasting site lists La Puerta Alta wines under La Rioja, Famatina and Mendoza, so the house also bottles Mendoza fruit: confirm the Torrontés taught is Famatina fruit. La Puerta Alta Bonarda and the sweet Torrontés go in others; awards are never told. The agronomist and the winemaker are living: name neither.

picks.why: A small family vineyard and artisan winery in the Valle de Huaco in the department of Sanagasta, about 1,250 metres up, the first extensive planting of its valley by its own account; its Malbec is a red of the province from outside the Famatina.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; not in the region record. Pick in doubt: the thinnest of the five. Found in the thin run on the province's tourism list (turismo.larioja.gob.ar, Finca Vista Larga, Valle de Huaco, Sanagasta), in Argentine press (bichosdecampo.com, the family project, Torrontés, Chardonnay, Malbec and Bonarda, and the valley's own geographical indication granted by the INV by resolution 6 of 2026: confirm the resolution before teaching it) and on Vivino, which lists six wines, the Malbec among them. No producer page was seen: confirm from the house that it bottles a Malbec under its own name, which wine it leads with (the Torrontés may be the truer pick) and the founding year, else leave founded empty. If the house cannot be confirmed, tell the merge agent: the province census holds few bottlers (19 cellars on the Ruta del Torrontés, 5 bottling their own brand, by argentina.gob.ar). Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: San Juan's historic house, dated by its own history to 1870 and the first vineyard planted under the name by an Italian immigrant; the Centenario Malbec, the reserve range of its export years, is the label by which the old name was met on lists.
picks.note: Answered: 1870 by the house's history, with 1869 for an uncle's purchase of land and 1876 for the founder's own cellar told beside it; the founder described, not named, his year of birth unsettled. The label is Graffigna Centenario Malbec, Tulum Valley fruit, listed to the 2016 vintage; whether it is still made is open. The sale to VSPT Wine Group is dated to its announcement of January 2019 by the San Juan press and the trade; the turn of 2022 towards Uco Valley fruit is told as partial. The Xumek swap was refused by the refuter and is not applied.

picks.why: A Tulum Valley house founded in 1993 that carried San Juan Syrah onto export lists; the Gran Syrah, blended from the Tulum, Zonda and Pedernal valleys, is its flagship and the province's grape at full stretch.
picks.note: Answered: 1993 by two guides, 1992 by one, and the three valleys of the Gran Syrah by the house's page; the eighteen months in new French and American oak by the house. Whether Gran Syrah or a wine above it leads the house stays the author's doubt. The Australian viticulturist is not named; Sagrado Pedernal and the rest are in others.

picks.why: A Tulum Valley estate at Caucete founded in 2002 by the Dutch family behind Bodegas Salentein and built around Syrah, the grape the province made its name with; its Magna Syrah, from the house's Tulum vineyards, is San Juan's warm style in the glass.
picks.note: Answered: the leading Syrah taught is the Magna Syrah, its fruit the house's own Tulum vineyards at Caucete by its sheets; 2002 by most sources, 2001 by one. Callia and Pyros are one family's two houses, each with its own cellar, valley and range, the Tulum and the Pedernal, so both stand; whether Pyros and Callia's Pedernal estate are one vineyard is open. Grand Callia and the Magna Malbec are in others; no member of the family is named.

picks.why: A Pedernal Valley estate at about 1,400 metres on the province's high western side, showing what altitude does for San Juan Malbec and Syrah; the Vineyard Block No. 4 Malbec, from one block of the estate, is its wine to know.
picks.note: Answered: the label is Pyros Single Vineyard Block No. 4 Malbec, the vineyard at about 1,400 metres on limestone and flint and the purchase and planting of 2008 by the house's sheets and Bonvivir; the 2021 sheet draws the wine from parts of parcels 3, 4 and 5. The Appellation Malbec and Syrah are in others. See Callia's note.

picks.why: A small project at Barreal in the Calingasta Valley, bottling old pergola Criolla and other heritage grapes from smallholders' vineyards under the Andes; its Criolla is the old mission grape of the Spanish made as a light, fresh red.
picks.note: Answered: the label is Cara Sur Criolla Chica, the form varying by vintage; Criolla Chica is the grape Chile calls País. The name is the south face of Cerro Mercedario; the project formed in 2011 by two couples, none named. Resolution 30 of 16 August 2024 of the National Wine Institute dated by the Boletín Oficial. The vines' planting year is unsettled and left out.

picks.why: Mainque estate in the Río Negro founded in 2004 around abandoned own rooted Pinot Noir and farmed biodynamically; Treinta y Dos, from the vines planted in 1932 and named for the year, showed that Argentina had more than Malbec to give.
picks.note: Answered: 2004 and the lease of the own rooted vineyard of 1932, the 1955 and 1967 vineyards and the biodynamic certification by the house's press kits, Sotheby's Wine and K&L; the first vintage of Treinta y Dos (2003, 2004 or 2006 by source) is not given. The founder is described as a member of the family behind Sassicaia; no living member named. Cincuenta y Cinco and Barda are in others.

picks.why: The historic Alto Valle house at General Roca, making wine since the early twentieth century; its Old Vineyard Sémillon, from the estate's old vines, is the Patagonian white a sommelier is asked about.
picks.note: Answered: 1909 at General Roca by the Río Negro newspaper, La Nación, Forbes Argentina and Mercado, the house's own domain giving nothing; the founder described, not named, his dates not found. The label is Old Vineyard Sémillon from Finca Milagros, planted in 1942; the La Morita Riesling of 1937 told in the story. No living member of the family named. The other wines are in others.

picks.why: A Río Negro estate built on an old own rooted Malbec parcel of the Alto Valle; Noemía, from that parcel, is the house's flagship and the wine that showed Patagonian Malbec of fine bones.
picks.note: Answered: the vineyard is at Mainqué, not Valle Azul, planted in 1932 on its own roots, and 2001 for the house, by its own page, Decanter and Wine Folly; organic, not biodynamic, farming, later certified; the year the vineyard was bought is not given. The founders are described, not named. J. Alberto and A Lisa are in others.

picks.why: A San Patricio del Chañar estate in Neuquén, whose cellar works uncovered a dinosaur fossil remembered in its Saurus range; the Saurus Pinot Noir is the range's red a guest meets on lists.
picks.note: Answered: 2001 by the house, the fossil a plant eating dinosaur described in 2010 as Panamericansaurus schroederi, and the first wine a Saurus Select Pinot Noir of 2003 by the house's pages; the refuter accepted the Saurus Pinot Noir over a Malbec. No living member of the family named; the upper range and the late harvest Pinot Noir are in others.

picks.why: The pioneering estate of San Patricio del Chañar, founded in 1999 by the developer behind the zone's planting, which planted the Neuquén desert for wine with Malbec and the grapes of Bordeaux; its Special Blend, of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, is the house's flagship red.
picks.note: Answered: 1999 for the founding and the first vineyards, the first harvest of 2002; the founder described as the zone's developer, not named. The Special Blend is Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, called the flagship red by one review, the head of the house's range unsettled; the Reserva form is cut, unsourced. Ownership left out; the Gran Reserva is in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Vicuña in the Elqui, founded in 1998 by two cousins, one a winemaker from Trentino, in a valley known until then for pisco grapes; its Syrah is the wine of the north a sommelier meets first.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run: founded in 1998 near Vicuña, Valle de Elqui, by two cousins, one of them an Italian winemaker who has made the wines since the start (South America Wine Guide, the importer Profile Wine Group, the Vicuña tourist office); name neither, both are living. The label is open: the house bottles Syrah as a Reserva, as Titón Reserva Syrah (Decanter lists a 2019) and as a Gran Reserva, and one merchant gives its Gran Reserva as a blend of Carménère and Syrah, so confirm from the house's own sheet which Syrah leads, how it is made and whether the Gran Reserva is Syrah alone, and keep Syrah in the name. The Titón vineyard also gives a Syrah under Mayu, the family's other Elqui label, which goes in others. Leave out the vineyard size quoted by the guides.

picks.why: A small estate in the upper Elqui at Alcohuaz, with vineyards between about 1,650 and 2,200 metres on granite, among the highest in Chile; Tococo is its Syrah from a parcel at about 1,800 metres.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run on the house's own site (alcohuaz.cl, read through search): vineyards from 1,650 to 2,206 metres, Tococo Syrah alone in the 2022 vintage; European Cellars and Berry Bros. list it as Tococo Syrah, Valle de Elqui, and a South American guide places its single parcel, planted in 2009, at 1,788 metres. One merchant says a 2020 Tococo carried Petite Sirah from a higher plot: tell the blend by vintage. Rhu, the house's other red, Syrah with some Petite Sirah from 1,750 to 2,206 metres by the house, goes in others. The lane's treading by foot and pressing by hand were not tested here: say them only from the house's sheet. The founding year and the family were not confirmed: leave founded empty unless two sources agree, and name no living person.

picks.why: A Limarí estate whose Talinay vineyard, on a raised marine terrace of limestone about 12 kilometres from the Pacific under the morning fog, gave the valley one of its first coastal Chardonnays; the Talinay Chardonnay is the wine of that site.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirmed in the thin run on the house's own data sheets (tabali.com, read through search): Talinay Chardonnay, DO Valle de Limarí, at 150 metres, 12 km from the sea, on limestone of an ancient marine terrace; Boutinot and The Wine Society give the same distance and the limestone (World of Fine Wine says about 10 km: use the house's figure). The founding year 2002 came from one search summary only: confirm from the house and a second source or leave founded empty, and name no founder, the family is living. The lane's line that Talinay defined the valley's Chardonnay was inflated and is gone. Talinay Caliza, the house's higher Chardonnay from the same site, and the Talinay Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc go in others.

picks.why: A Maipo house founded in 1885 at Talagante, here for its Limarí wine: the T.H. Chardonnay of its Terroir Hunter range comes from Quebrada Seca in the west of the valley, a large house's reading of the north.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. A large house's local wine, said so plainly: its home is the Maipo. Confirmed in the thin run: founded in 1885 at Talagante, the estate first called Fundo Santa Ana after the founder's wife, by the house's own history page and Wikipedia; the founder is long dead and may be named only with his dates from two sources. The label is T.H. [Terroir Hunter] Chardonnay, D.O. Valle de Limarí, from Quebrada Seca, by Decanter's reviews across several vintages, Wine Enthusiast and a Brazilian merchant, which gives ten months on lees in concrete and 500 litre French oak for the 2022: confirm the regime from the house's sheet and tell it by vintage. Leave out the vineyard size the merchants quote. Its Maipo wines go in others.

picks.why: A house created by Concha y Toro in 1993 with its winery at Chimbarongo in Colchagua, here for its Limarí wine: the 20 Barrels Limited Edition Syrah comes from its Los Almendros estate in the valley.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. A fifth pick added in the thin run, another large house's local wine, said so plainly. Confirmed: Cono Sur created in 1993 by Concha y Toro, by the parent's own timeline and Wikipedia, its base at Chimbarongo; the 20 Barrels Limited Edition Syrah from the Los Almendros estate in the Limarí, by the SAQ, a Bottlebooks sheet from the house and a critic's published note on the 2017, and listed as Limarí in vintages from 2008 to 2022 (Firstleaf, WineAlign, IWSC). The blend moves by vintage (97 per cent Syrah with Cabernet Sauvignon in 2017; Syrah with Cabernet Sauvignon and Carménère in 2022): tell it by vintage, and confirm the barrel regime from the house's sheet. The house's 20 Barrels wines from other valleys go in others or nowhere. Present ownership is volatile: tell the creation in 1993 as history.

swaps.why: the house's own sheets call Alazán its flagship Pinot Noir, Tobiano being its other original, lighter label; house and key kept

picks.why: Founded at Panquehue in 1870, the historic house of the Aconcagua valley; Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve, its Cabernet Sauvignon led blend named for the founder, is the house's flagship and the valley's red to know.
picks.note: Answered: 1870 and the founder's dates (1832 to 1890) by the Chilean Congress library and a second source, so he is named with them. The Founder's Reserve was first released with the 1984 vintage, Cabernet Sauvignon alone, by Decanter and The World of Fine Wine, and became a blend led by Cabernet; a 1983 listed by one merchant stays open. The Max blocks and the oak follow the house's sheets, by vintage. Seña is in others and a trap as the separate estate begun with the Mondavi winery; Las Pizarras is in others. The family head is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Estate founded in 2000 at Lo Abarca in the San Antonio Valley, four kilometres from the Pacific, which took Chilean Sauvignon Blanc to the edge of the ocean; the Cipreses Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc is its single vineyard wine to know.
picks.note: Answered: 2000, Lo Abarca and the four kilometres from the sea by the house and the record's other sources; the first woman to found and own a Chilean winery is told as the house's claim. Lo Abarca as a denomination of one producer from 2018 rests on the house and two trade sources, the decree itself unread. The Miramar Vineyard Syrah and Riesling are in others. The founder and her son are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Founded in the late 1990s, the house that brought Maipo river water to the Leyda hills and planted the zone that bears its name; the Lot 21 Pinot Noir, of the house's small lot line drawn from a selection of its plots, is the zone's red to know, beside its Sauvignon Blanc.
picks.note: Answered: founded is empty, 1998 in most accounts and 1997 in one, so the story says the late 1990s; the pipeline, the planting of 1998, the Leyda Valley of 2002 and the sale to the San Pedro group in 2007 are told as history. Lot 21 is taught over the Garuma Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc, which is in others with Las Brisas. Open: no technical sheet of the house for Lot 21 was found, so its making is hedged. The winemaker is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A biodynamic estate in the Rosario valley between Casablanca and San Antonio, whose EQ Syrah showed that cool coastal Chile could make peppery reds in the northern Rhône manner.
picks.note: Answered: the Rosario valley planted in 1999, the first harvest of 2001, organic certification and biodynamic farming from 2004 by the house; EQ Syrah carries the San Antonio Valley denomination. The question whether the Matetic Syrah stands above EQ was refused by the refuter: Decanter calls EQ the house's premium label, so the plan stands. Chile's first cool climate Syrah is told as the house's claim; the Demeter year is left out. The EQ Pinot Noir, the EQ Coastal Sauvignon Blanc and Corralillo are in others. The family member who planted the valley is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A Casablanca estate in the western hills of the valley, planted on the family's ranch in 1998 and known for Pinot Noir and cool Syrah; Alazán, its flagship Pinot Noir blended from barrel selected lots and aged in French oak, concrete eggs and Austrian foudres, is its Casablanca red to know.
picks.note: Answered: the planting of 1998 and the first own label of 2003 by the family's account; renamed on 2026-11-21 from Tobiano to Alazán, which the house's 2021 sheet calls its flagship Pinot Noir; Tobiano, the other original label, is in others. The second reader cut the tiering of lots (Alazán from the first choice, Tobiano the next), found on no page of the house. The name for a family horse of deep red coat is the house's account; the oak, about a third new, and the vessels on its Pinot Noir page and sheets, eight to eleven months by vintage. Open: the first vintage of Alazán (2003 on a writer's own site only) is not dated, and the house's claim of a decade in bottle is left out. A larger Casablanca house in Kingston's place was refused for now. The family member who led the move into wine, the uncle who owned the horse and the consulting winemaker are never named.

picks.why: The Penedès family's Chilean house, at Curicó since 1979 and among the first in Chile to ferment in stainless steel at controlled temperatures; Manso de Velasco, first made in 1985 from a Curicó vineyard of Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1902 on its own roots by the house's account, and named for the governor who founded the city, was its first premium wine.
picks.note: Answered: not joined to p-torres, and the record says Miguel Torres Chile is the family's separate Chilean company. The vineyard near Molina, planted in 1902 by the house's account and bought in 1984, the first vintage of 1985 and the governor (about 1688 to 1767) who founded Curicó on 9 October 1743, by the record's sources; the oak moves by vintage and the record says so. The stainless steel is told as among the first, not as the first. Escaleras de Empedrado, which several sources set above Manso de Velasco in the house's Chilean range, is in others with the Cordillera Carignan and Santa Digna, and the integrator may weigh it. The house's winemakers are listed in people.json; the family is never named.

picks.why: Founded in 1879 as Champagne Valdivieso by the house's account, the country's historic sparkling house, its still wines made later at its Lontué winery in the Curicó; Caballo Loco, a red with no vintage, each release half new wine and half a reserve kept back from the one before in the manner of a solera, and numbered by release, is the house's wine a sommelier is asked about.
picks.note: Answered: 1879 and the sparkling start rest on the house's account; one book places that founding at Santa Elena, and the still wines of Lontué came much later, so the record no longer places 1879 at Lontué. Caballo Loco was launched in 1994, half bottled and half kept back, by Decanter and Just Drinks; Number 20 is the anniversary release. The founder is not named for want of dates; the makers of the first numbers are listed in people.json. The sparkling wines, the Grand Cru wines and the Blanco are in others.

picks.why: A Maule family house of French origin at Mingre in the dry farmed secano and a leader of the País revival; País Salvaje comes from wild vines that climb into the trees and is fermented with native yeasts.
picks.note: Answered: the house trades as Bouchon Family Wines and labels as J. Bouchon; the founder, a Bordeaux winemaker who crossed to Chile in the late nineteenth century, is described, his year and dates not found. País Salvaje is told with the Drinks Business's correction of 2015 in favour of Villalobos. Organic farming is the house's account, the certification left out as volatile, and VIGNO is joined after its founding. Open: the family's year of arrival and the purchase of Mingre. The white País Salvaje, the País Viejo and the house's Vigno are in others. The living father and son of one name and the present generation are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A small house making wines from tiny parcels of smallholders in the Maule and Itata, and a member of VIGNO; its Truquilemu Carignan, from old dry farmed bush vines of the Maule secano, is the Carignan revival in one bottle.
picks.note: Answered: the label is Cru Truquilemu Carignan, the vineyard's own selection, accepted by the refuter over the lot bottling, which is in others with the house's Vigno and the Old Vine Pale. The beginning of 2001 by the house and a second source; the newspaper's naming and the export of 2006 rest on the house alone and are told as its account. VIGNO was legally constituted in 2011. The founders are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A house of a Norwegian shipping family, farmed organically, with old dry farmed Carignan at Cauquenes in the Maule secano; its Orzada Carignan is that Maule Carignan in the house's hands.
picks.note: Answered: founded is empty, the purchase at Padre Hurtado and the first plantings told without a date; the gravity flow winery of 1997 in the Maipo (Alliance Wine, BusinessMirror), the Armador range of 1999 and the first varietal Carignan of 2001 by the record's sources. Orzada's making follows the house's 2021 sheet, which names no barrel. Odfjell is a member of VIGNO, its joining undated. The founder, a guard for prose, and the son who designed the winery are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: The Isla de Maipo house founded in 1934 whose old vine Cinsault and País from Itata, fermented and aged in old clay tinajas, led the south's revival on export lists; the Viejas Tinajas Cinsault is that wine.
picks.note: Answered: 1934 by the house; the year the tinajas were bought is cut, and the first Viejas Tinajas of the 2011 vintage by three merchants and the reviews, against the house's own count that would start the series in 2012, which stays open. Guarilihue's granite and the Secano Interior label until the decree of 2015 (Decree 7, read in the Congress library). Recent vintages are labelled Viejas Tinajas Tinto with some whole bunches, a rename left for the integrator, the plan's name kept as the long standing label. The founder is described for want of dates; the third and fourth generations are listed in people.json. Gallardía del Itata, the Muscat and the Maipo Carmenère are in others.

picks.why: An Itata project built on smallholders' dry farmed bush vines, bottling old vine Cinsault, País and Moscatel at modest alcohol; the Grand Itata Tinto, mostly Cinsault with a little País, is the dry granite hills of Itata in a glass.
picks.note: Answered: begun in 2011 by two founders in a garage in Concepción; Cinsault with about five per cent País from Guarilihue vines of 1960 by the importers' sheets, fermented in concrete, against the house's own page naming Carignan too, which stays open. The Grand Itata Blanco and the Super Itata Tinto are in others, the latter's grapes unconfirmed. The founders are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A Maipo house founded with Bordeaux partners, here for its far southern wine: the Sol de Sol Chardonnay, from vines first planted in 1993 at Traiguén in the Malleco and first made with the 2000 vintage, by the house's account from the zone's first vineyard.
picks.note: Answered: the search of 1984, the Quebrada de Macul bought in 1990 and the winery of 1993, the Traiguén planting of 1993 on the land of the Chilean partner's father in law and the first vintage of 2000 by the house's pages and the record's other sources; the Champagne partner of 2002. The first vineyard of the zone and the wine's part in the Malleco's denomination are the house's claims, told as such; the decree's year was not found. The Sol de Sol Pinot Noir exists by the house's pages and is in others. The founders are described, the one who died in 2016 not named, and the living partners are listed in people.json.

picks.why: A family cellar at Yumbel in the Bío Bío with vines said to go back to the eighteenth century, known for traditional pipeño, the light, rustic País of the southern countryside; its Pipeño is that old country wine bottled for lists.
picks.note: Answered: founded is empty; the seven generations and the País of 1776 are the family's account, another giving the 1760s, and the name's Mapuche origin is told as the family tells it. Yumbel in the dry inland hills of the Bío Bío, the Secano Interior taught by the decree of 2015. The Pipeño is País fermented in open raulí vats, bottled in a litre. The Vino Naranja and the Naturalmente Tinto are in others. The grower is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: A natural wine grower of Concepción working old País and Moscatel vines in the Bío Bío and Itata near the Nahuelbuta range; Rivera del Notro, red País from the Bío Bío, is the old mission grape made in the manner of the new south.
picks.note: Answered: the house keeps the grower's own name, and the record says no more of him than the grower; out on his own in 2015 by his own biography, his vineyards worked on long agreements with their owners. The red Rivera del Notro, País from Nacimiento, is taught, raised in neutral vessels with no new oak; the white of Moscatel, Corinto and Sémillon is in others with Santa Cruz de Coya and País Franco. The Loire grower and the French winemaker in Chile beside him are listed in people.json and never named. Open: the vineyard's soil, alluvial over dark sand.

picks.why: Auburn house of 1981 that bottles its dry Rieslings by site; Polish Hill, from shallow shale over blue slate in the Polish Hill River locality, is the tighter and slower to open of its pair beside Springvale.
picks.note: Answered: 1981 and the old milk depot at Auburn by the house, the house's own Polish Hill vineyard planted in 1996, and the screwcap of 2000 told as the house leading fourteen Clare producers. The first Polish Hill came with the 1981 wines; the fruit before 1996 is not named (open). Springvale and Gaia are in others. Watervale and Polish Hill are called localities, never subregions. The founder is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Clare family house of 1959; The Armagh is its single vineyard Shiraz, the proof that the Riesling valley also makes dense, long lived red.
picks.note: Answered: the founder named with his death in 2004 at seventy nine, his birth year open; the land of 1964, the Shiraz planted at the end of the 1960s from Wendouree cuttings by most accounts, the first The Armagh of 1985 in new American oak and French oak later, by the house's vintage journal. The Florita, bought from Lindemans in 1986, is in the story. The founder's sons and the family are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Sevenhill property with dry grown vines dating in part from the 1890s, sold almost wholly by mailing list; its Shiraz is the dense, tannic, slow ageing Clare red the house is known for.
picks.note: Answered: founded left empty; the first vines of 1892 or 1893, the first wines of 1895, the handover of 1917 and the mortgagee sale of 1974 told. Open: whether the son's winemaking ended in 1970 or 1983. The house makes reds only. The couple who have run it since 1974 and the buyer of that year are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: The winery Austrian Jesuits founded at Sevenhill in 1851 to make sacramental wine, by its own account the oldest of the valley; St Ignatius is its red blend of Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc.
picks.note: Answered: the land and the first vines of 1851 by the house, wine five years later by the house and a first prize at Auburn in 1858; the oldest winery of the valley told as the house's claim. The pick in doubt stands: St Ignatius is the house's long running blend named for the order's founder, and its refuter refused the reserve Shiraz as a swap. Open: the first vintage of St Ignatius and its months in oak.

picks.why: Auburn house named for Mount Horrocks, which honours the valley's pioneer of the 1840s; Cordon Cut is its sweet Riesling, made by cutting the canes so the fruit dries on the vine, the valley's other face beside its dry Riesling.
picks.note: Answered: founded left empty; John Ainsworth Horrocks with his dates, the purchase of 1993, the railway station cellar door of 1998 and Cordon Cut still made under that name, more than twenty vintages by 2014. Open: the first vintage of Cordon Cut. The owner since 1993 is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: McLaren Vale family house of 1912 that still foot treads and basket presses; The Dead Arm is its Shiraz, named for the vine disease that withers one arm of an old vine and leaves the other to bear.
picks.note: Answered: 1912 and the son's own winery of the late 1920s; d'Arry Osborn named with his dates (1926 to 2022); The Dead Arm told as the early 1990s, the name in 1993 and Shiraz alone from 1994 by Decanter. The founder is described, not named. d'Arry's children are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: House founded in 1894 and revived at the end of the 1960s; RSW Shiraz, named with the founder's initials, heads its range, beside the Church Block red blend a guest is more likely to have met.
picks.note: Answered: 1894 and Robert Strangways Wigley (1864 to 1926, one summary giving another year of death, open); the revival at the end of the 1960s by two cousins and Church Block of 1972 by the house. RSW's first vintage is not settled and stays out. The surviving cousin and the maker who reworked Church Block are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Company founded in 1853 whose founder bought the Tintara winery at McLaren Vale in 1876; Eileen Hardy Shiraz, named for the widow who held the family firm together after 1938, was first released in 1973 from the 1970 vintage and is drawn from chosen parcels of old McLaren Vale Shiraz.
picks.note: Answered: Thomas Hardy (1830 to 1912), Bankside of 1853 by the house (1854 in one account), Tintara bought in 1876; the first Eileen Hardy Shiraz from the 1970 vintage, released in 1973 for her eightieth birthday, by the house's account. Open: whether early vintages drew on fruit beyond McLaren Vale, told by one columnist only; the record says nothing of it.

picks.why: Family winery of 1890 at Amery; Block 6 Shiraz comes from a hillside planted in 1892, part of whose first vines survive.
picks.note: Answered: Amery bought in 1890 and the purchase completed in 1891, Block 6 planted in 1892 from Tintara cuttings with part of it surviving, the first single vineyard bottling of the mid 1980s (1984 or 1985 by the house's pages). The label reads Kay Brothers. The family member who first bottled it is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Biodynamic estate at Blewitt Springs; High Sands is its Grenache from bush vines planted in 1946 on the district's deep sand, the old vine Grenache that is the region's second voice beside Shiraz.
picks.note: Answered: founded left empty; Block 31 planted in 1946 (1947 in one account), Eringa Park bought at the turn of the century from the break up of Normans Wines by the family company behind Kendall-Jackson, the first High Sands of 2005 and certification since 2012. Nobody of the house is named.

picks.why: Lilydale estate of 1971 whose wines have kept to a restrained style; Quintet, the house's blend of the five Bordeaux varieties, is named for the five.
picks.note: Answered: John Middleton (1924 to 2006) named with his dates, the planting of 1971 and the first commercial release of Quintet in 1976 by the house's account. The founder's wife stays unnamed. The family's living members are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Gruyere estate founded in 1969, one of the estates that began the valley's revival; Dry Red Wine No. 1 is its Cabernet led Bordeaux blend, with the Shiraz led No. 2 as its counterpart.
picks.note: Answered: the founder, a botanist trained in plant physiology who worked for the CSIRO, is described, not named, for want of a birth year in two sources; the label reads Dry Red Wine No. 1, a Cabernet led blend with Merlot, Malbec and Petit Verdot. The winemakers are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Estate founded in 1863 by a Swiss settler, who began its vineyard there, and replanted from 1969 by his grandson on the same ground; the red named Yeringberg, led by Cabernet Sauvignon, is its flagship, beside a Marsanne and Roussanne white.
picks.note: Answered: Guillaume de Pury (1831 to 1890) named with his dates; 1863, the winery of 1885 to 1891 by the heritage register, the last vintage of 1921 and the replanting of 1969 by his grandson; the red's label is the estate's name alone. The grandson is listed in people.json as a guard, his death not settled, and never named.

picks.why: Coldstream house founded in 1985 by a wine writer to make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; its Reserve Pinot Noir is the wine of the house a guest is most likely to know by name.
picks.note: Answered: 1985, the first vintage chiefly of bought grapes by the founder's account, Southcorp in 1996, Foster's in 2005 and Treasury Wine Estates in 2011. Open: the Reserve's first vintage, and its months in oak, which differ by sheet. The founder and his wife are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Moët & Chandon's Australian house, founded in 1986 at Green Point by Coldstream to make traditional method sparkling wine; its Vintage Brut, by the house's account the first wine made there, is the one to know.
picks.note: Answered: the label reads Chandon, the house long Domaine Chandon and now Chandon Australia; Green Point an old dairy farm by the house, and 1986 as its own date. The fruit grows mostly at Whitlands and in the Strathbogie Ranges, which the record teaches; its refuter refused the swap to Yering Station, left to the integrator. Open: the label's Geographical Indication.

picks.why: Family house of 1858 whose Rare Muscat is blended from reserves laid down over generations, the highest rung of the Rutherglen ladder.
picks.note: Answered: 1858, the rose hedge and the replanting on rootstock from 1901 by the house; the solera on base wines of the 1890s and 1900 hedged as the house's; Bill Chambers named with his dates (1933 to 2023); Tokay phased out by the agreement of 2008 and off Australian labels in 2020, the Muscadelle labelled by its grape. The label reads Rare Rutherglen Muscat. Open: the solera's age, which the house's pages give two ways, and the serving figure. The sixth generation is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: House of 1859 with one of the district's deep reserve cellars; Old Premium Rare Muscat is its release at the Rare rung, drawn from those old reserves.
picks.note: Answered: George Francis Morris (1834 to 1910) named with his dates, land of 1859 and the trial vineyard by the house's account, Mia Mia of 1897 and the prize horse, the sale around 1970, Pernod Ricard from 1989 and Casella Family Brands in 2016; the label reads Old Premium Liqueur Muscat. Open: the trial plot of 1859, the dictionary giving Brown's Plain land of 1860. The family member living is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Family house whose first vintage came in 1870; its Rare wines carry names of their own: Merchant Prince, after the ship that brought the founder, is its Rare Muscat, beside Isabella, its Rare Topaque.
picks.note: Answered: the voyage of 1857, the arrival of 1860 and the first vintage of 1870 told as the family's account; Merchant Prince launched in 1983 and Isabella in 1990 by the house's timeline, Isabella a Topaque since Tokay was phased out; the Bobbie Burns Shiraz in the story. The oldest base wine cut. Open: the solera's average age, the house's over fifty against merchants' fifty to sixty. The family members living are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Wahgunyah estate of 1864 on the Murray by its own account, founded by two friends from Caithness, its castle winery recalling the Castle of Mey; its Rare Muscat is the house's wine at the highest rung of the Rutherglen ladder.
picks.note: Answered: 1864 as the estate's own date, the castle left undated and its likeness held to the estate's word (the battlements and the turrets), the parish naming cut; the Brown family in the 1990s. The pick in doubt is upheld by its refuter: the Rare stands at the fourth rung, the Museum Muscat filled to order in very small numbers. The founders are described, not named, for want of agreed dates. The Brown siblings are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Rutherglen house of 1875 known for a fortified red of a single year made in the manner of Vintage Port; its Vintage Fortified joins Shiraz and Durif to Portuguese grapes such as Touriga Nacional.
picks.note: Answered: the first official vintage of 1875, the name Stanton and Killeen of 1968, the Portuguese plantings through the 1980s and 1990s by the sixth generation winemaker, who died in 2007, and Port closed to Australian labels by the agreements with the European Union. The 2002 label year cut. The pick in doubt is upheld by its refuter, the house's pages making vintage fortified its style. The living owners are listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Tasmanian house built on vintage sparkling wine aged for years on its lees; Grand Vintage, its core vintage cuvée of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, is the wine to know beside the late disgorged releases above it.
picks.note: Answered: 1995 in four sources; the visit of 1988 by the sparkling winemaker who later joined Hardys, the name a word for tapestry, the first Arras wine of the 1995 harvest released in 1999, six years and more of tirage by the house's spec lines, and the sale of 2023 to Handpicked Wines. The late disgorged release is never called by its name. The founding winemaker is listed in people.json and never named.

picks.why: Pipers River house born of a partnership of 1986 between Louis Roederer and Heemskerk Wines and made for traditional method sparkling wine alone; Premium Cuvée is its non vintage, from the estate vineyard with fruit from other Tasmanian sites.
picks.note: Answered: Heemskerk planted in 1975 (the library's, open), the Roederer partnership of 1986, the Hill-Smith family's purchase of 1998 (1997 in two accounts), eighteen months and more on lees by the house; Abel Janszoon Tasman with his dates. picks.why: The Robertson house begun on the Madeba farm in 1983 and given wholly to Cap Classique on lime-rich soils since the middle of the 2010s; its non-vintage Brut, from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, was poured at Nelson Mandela's inauguration in 1994 and is the wine a guest knows.
picks.note: The library holds the house and the Brut. Confirm the inauguration story and its year from two sources, and the founder's dates from two sources before naming him. Name no living cellar master. Cuvée Clive, the prestige wine, and the Blanc de Blancs belong in others.

picks.why: A family Chardonnay house on the lime soils, among the Cape's pioneers of the grape; Bateleur, named for the eagle of the African skies, is its barrel fermented Chardonnay.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched: confirm from the house's own pages that Bateleur heads its range (beside The Site), its first vintage and the family's history on the farm, from two sources. The family members are living: say the family.

picks.why: A family farm on stony river soils known for Sauvignon Blanc and a wild yeast Chardonnay; Life from Stone, named for the rock strewn ground of its vineyard, is the Sauvignon Blanc the house is known by.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched: confirm the label's exact words, the soils, the farm's history and the founding year from two sources. Name no living family member. The Wild Yeast Chardonnay and Méthode Ancienne belong in others.

picks.why: The Burger family's estate since 1864; the 1908 Muscadel is a fortified Red Muscadel from a small block of bush vines planted in 1908, which the house calls the oldest of its kind in South Africa.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own page sells the wine. Hedge the claim of the oldest vines as the house's. Confirm who planted the block (told as a second generation Burger aged seventy) and the purchaser of 1864 (named Alwyn and Alewyn) from two sources before naming either. No size of the block or the farm.
